clinicalPearls: A myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by a sustained rise in platelet count from clonal overproduction of megakaryocytes
Many patients are asymptomatic and detected on a routine blood count, while others present with vasomotor symptoms such as headache, erythromelalgia (burning red extremities), and visual disturbance
Both arterial and venous thrombosis and, paradoxically, bleeding can occur; bleeding risk rises with very high platelet counts due to acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency
Most cases carry a driver mutation in JAK2, CALR, or MPL, which supports clonality and helps distinguish ET from reactive thrombocytosis
Reactive causes of a high platelet count (iron deficiency, infection, inflammation, malignancy, post-splenectomy) must be excluded before diagnosing ET
Treatment intensity is guided by thrombotic risk, factoring in age, prior thrombosis, and JAK2 status; low-dose aspirin is used for microvascular symptoms and thrombosis prevention
Cytoreduction (for example with hydroxyurea) is reserved for higher-risk patients to lower the platelet count and reduce thrombotic events
Long-term risks include transformation to myelofibrosis or, less commonly, acute leukaemia
reference.pathophysiology: ET is a clonal disorder of the haematopoietic stem cell in which constitutive activation of the JAK-STAT signalling pathway, most often through JAK2 V617F, CALR, or MPL mutations, drives excessive megakaryocyte proliferation and platelet production independent of normal regulatory signals. The expanded platelet mass and qualitatively abnormal platelets promote thrombosis in the microcirculation and larger vessels. At very high counts, platelets adsorb and clear large von Willebrand factor multimers, producing an acquired von Willebrand syndrome and a paradoxical bleeding tendency. Over years the clone may evolve towards marrow fibrosis or acute leukaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Reactive (secondary) thrombocytosis from iron deficiency, infection, or inflammation
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film to confirm sustained thrombocytosis and assess morphology
Molecular testing for JAK2 V617F, and if negative, CALR and MPL mutations
BCR-ABL1 testing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine showing enlarged, clustered megakaryocytes
Iron studies, inflammatory markers, and screening for occult malignancy to exclude reactive causes
Assessment for acquired von Willebrand syndrome when counts are very high or bleeding occurs
redFlags: Acute arterial or venous thrombosis, including stroke, myocardial infarction, or splanchnic vein thrombosis
Significant haemorrhage, particularly with extreme thrombocytosis and acquired von Willebrand deficiency
Transient neurological or visual symptoms indicating microvascular ischaemia
Features of transformation to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia such as worsening cytopenias or new blasts
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy in ET is close to that of the general population for many patients, with the principal threats being thrombosis and haemorrhage; a minority progress over years to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia, which markedly worsens outlook.
pitfalls: Diagnosing ET without excluding reactive thrombocytosis and chronic myeloid leukaemia
Prescribing aspirin at very high platelet counts without recognising acquired von Willebrand syndrome and bleeding risk
Underestimating thrombotic risk in JAK2-positive or older patients
Attributing microvascular symptoms to unrelated causes and missing the underlying disorder
Failing to reassess for transformation when the blood picture changes
management: Low-dose aspirin for vasomotor and microvascular symptoms and thrombosis prevention, provided acquired von Willebrand syndrome is excluded
Risk-adapted platelet-lowering cytoreduction, using hydroxycarbamide first-line with interferon-alfa or anagrelide as alternatives, guided by age, prior thrombosis and JAK2 status
Modify thrombotic risk factors such as smoking, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia
Suspend antiplatelet therapy and manage the acquired von Willebrand syndrome when bleeding occurs at very high counts
Serial monitoring of the full blood count and surveillance for progression to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia
Ongoing haematology review with individualised risk reassessment
